title: Gold dips below $4,000 in worst week in four months as oil fuels Fed hike fears
body: With a Fed hold widely expected, gold's next move hinges on tone: any signal that a December hike remains live would likely lift yields and the dollar and push bullion back below $4,000, while a more balanced message could trigger a relief bounce from oversold levels. Oil is the key transmission channel, and further escalation in the Middle East that lifts crude would likely weigh on gold through higher inflation and rate expectations rather than support it as a haven. A softer PCE print on Thursday would offer the clearest route to a short-covering rally. Silver and gold miners, which underperformed last week, are likely to move with higher beta in either direction. --- Not gold, but interesting: Bitcoin ETF inflows fade as price pressure tests ETF buyers' $81,300 cost basis Strategy bitcoin purchases shrink as buybacks take priority ahead of earnings Bitcoin buyers are fighting back, but sellers aren't finished. Here are the two prices swing traders should watch --- Gold is being sold on the very geopolitical risk that once lifted it, as oil-driven inflation fears keep Fed hikes in play, leaving $4,000 as the line to watch in a pivotal week.

title: Bitcoin ETF inflows fade as price pressure tests ETF buyers' $81,300 cost basis
body: Bitcoin ETF demand returned last week, then faded. Now price is testing the ETF buyers' cost basis Money came back into US spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds last week, but it didn't stay. The funds took in about $1.07 billion over the first three sessions, then lost $773.5 million over the final two, according to preliminary Farside data. That left a provisional net inflow of $301.2 million for the week to October 23. Bitcoin, meanwhile, slipped back toward $80,000, close to the level where the average ETF buyer would start losing money. --- Earlier: Bitcoin buyers are fighting back, but sellers aren't finished. Here are the two prices swing traders should watch Strategy bitcoin purchases shrink as buybacks take priority ahead of earnings --- What happened The week opened strongly. Spot bitcoin ETFs took in $526.7 million on Monday, $23.2 million on Tuesday and $524.8 million on Wednesday. BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) led the way, drawing $665.2 million on Monday, its largest single-day inflow since October 2025. The mood then reversed. Thursday brought $635.6 million in outflows, the largest daily withdrawal since June, followed by another $137.9 million on Friday. IBIT itself saw $254.1 million leave on Thursday and $110.3 million on Friday, though it still finished the week with net inflows of $565.7 million. The week did end a run of two straight weeks of outflows. Even so, US spot bitcoin ETFs remain about $313.5 million in net outflows for October so far.

title: Bank of Canada preview: 81% chance of first hike in a year to 2.50%, economists split
body: With a hike close to fully priced, the Canadian dollar's reaction will likely turn on the Monetary Policy Report and forward guidance rather than the decision itself. A hold would be a sizeable surprise, likely sending the loonie sharply lower and pulling short-dated Canadian yields down. A hike signalling further tightening would support the currency and push the front end higher, while a "one and watch" message could see pricing for a follow-up move by March trimmed. Oil is the external wildcard: higher crude both lifts Canadian headline inflation and supports the commodity-linked loonie, so further energy price gains would reinforce the hawkish case. Friday's August GDP data could then quickly test whatever guidance the bank delivers. --- Busy week ahead (and I haven't even mentioned the elephant in the room yet!) BOJ preview: Daiwa sees hold, but 2% inflation call could open door to December hike Preview: RBNZ set to lift OCR to 3% ahead of election as oil and weak kiwi fuel inflation --- A week ago the Bank of Canada looked set to sit tight, but one hint from Governor Macklem about higher inflation forecasts has put a first hike in a year firmly on the table.

title: Standard Chartered sees debt-funded share of AI capex rising to 40% in 2027 from 25%
body: A growing reliance on debt to fund AI infrastructure ties the tech trade more closely to the rates outlook, so hawkish central bank signals, including a Fed on a hiking path, could weigh harder on capex-heavy names than in earlier phases of the boom. Credit markets are likely to see heavier tech bond issuance, and investors may demand wider spreads if deployment delays push back revenue. Next week's Big Tech results are the near-term catalyst: firm capex guidance paired with clearer monetisation would ease funding concerns, while rising spend without visible returns could deepen the mixed share-price reactions already evident. The bank's preference for diversification points to potential rotation toward sectors and regions outside concentrated US tech leadership. --- --- The AI build-out is increasingly running on borrowed money, and Standard Chartered wants proof of returns from Big Tech before adding to riskier corners of the sector.

title: BOJ preview: Daiwa sees hold, but 2% inflation call could open door to December hike
body: A hold is largely the base case, so the yen and JGB yields are likely to take their cue from the language rather than the decision. A formal declaration that underlying inflation has reached 2%, a Takata dissent and any shift by Ueda toward "next meeting" phrasing would together read as hawkish, supporting the yen and pushing short-end yields higher as markets price a December move. Higher crude prices are a key upside risk, with oil already reigniting upstream cost pressure and feeding the BOJ's concern about inflation overshooting. A guarded Ueda who stresses a broad review of financial conditions could see December pricing trimmed and the yen soften. --- Also this week: Preview: RBNZ set to lift OCR to 3% ahead of election as oil and weak kiwi fuel inflation --- The BOJ is expected to stand pat on rates while quietly moving the goalposts, from getting inflation up to 2% to stopping it from running beyond it, which keeps December firmly in play.

title: Brazil ETF tumbles nearly 15% in Tokyo after Lula's comeback runoff win
body: The Tokyo ETF move is an early and thin-volume signal, so the real test comes when Brazilian markets open, with the real, the local rates curve and the Bovespa likely to bear the brunt of any repricing. Goldman Sachs' figures describe an extreme scenario rather than a base case, but they frame the scale of the potential move, with the long end of the curve and the currency most exposed. Positioning matters: markets rallied after the first round on expectations of a different outcome, so some of the selling may reflect that trade being unwound rather than a fresh view on policy. Spillover to other Latin American currencies and EM risk sentiment is possible if the selloff is disorderly, while a contained reaction could see dip-buyers emerge quickly. --- Lula pulled off a rare second-round comeback, and the first verdict from markets, a near 15% drop in a Tokyo-listed Brazil ETF, suggests investors had been positioned for the other result.

title: Saudi Arabia to store crude in Singapore caverns from 2027 as Hormuz disruption bites
body: The arrangement will not add barrels before the second half of 2027, so the near-term price impact is limited, but it signals that producers and consumers expect Strait of Hormuz risk to persist well beyond the current war. Storage closer to Asian refiners would give Saudi Arabia a buffer to keep supplying key customers during future disruptions, helping defend its market share in the region against rival suppliers. Over time, a strategic stockpile in Singapore could reduce the risk premium Asian buyers pay during supply scares and strengthen the city-state's role as a regional pricing and trading hub. For now, oil markets remain driven by the immediate disruption to Hormuz flows, which this deal does not address. --- With the Strait of Hormuz no longer a safe bet, Saudi Arabia is planning to park its crude on Asia's doorstep.

title: Goldman's 79-tonne central bank gold estimate goes mainstream as reserves shift to London
body: Heavy official-sector buying offers a structural cushion beneath gold just as speculative liquidation has dragged prices below $4,000, and it supports the argument that dips are being absorbed by long-term buyers. It does not guarantee a floor, however: near-term direction still depends on oil, yields and Fed expectations, and central bank demand did not prevent last week's slide. The gap between Goldman's flow-based estimate and officially reported purchases suggests accumulation may be larger than disclosed, which matters for the longer-run supply-demand balance. The shift of holdings from New York to London is a reserve-management story rather than an immediate price driver, but it adds to debate over the dollar's role in official portfolios. --- Earlier: Gold dips below $4,000 as long liquidation swamps ETF buying, Saxo Bank says Gold dips below $4,000 in worst week in four months as oil fuels Fed hike fears --- While speculators dump gold, central banks are quietly buying it at a multiple of their old pace, and some are deciding they would rather keep it in London than New York.

title: ECB set to hold at 2.50% as Morgan Stanley sees December as natural moment for next hike
body: With a hold almost fully priced, the euro's reaction will turn on whether Lagarde validates December hike expectations or keeps full optionality, and a noncommittal message could see some tightening priced out and weigh on the single currency. The Fed decision a day earlier sets the backdrop for EUR/USD, so a hawkish Fed followed by a cautious ECB would be the most euro-negative combination. Higher oil linked to the Middle East conflict remains the main upside risk to eurozone inflation and to hike pricing. French government bonds are exposed to any sign that the ECB sees the recent rise in yields as a concern rather than welcome tightening, and Friday's flash inflation and GDP data could quickly reprice December either way. --- Earlier: ING sees BOJ holding at 1.25%, two hikes in 2027 Bank of Canada preview: 81% chance of first hike in a year to 2.50%, economists split BOJ preview: Daiwa sees hold, but 2% inflation call could open door to December hike Preview: RBNZ set to lift OCR to 3% ahead of election as oil and weak kiwi fuel inflation --- The ECB looks set to take a breather this week, letting higher bond yields do some of its work, while December shapes up as the meeting where the next hike gets decided.

A sustained climb in oil would also reinforce imported inflation, complicating the BOJ's preference to wait and potentially pulling hike expectations forward from January. With a hold fully priced, the yen and JGB yields are likely to react to guidance rather than the decision, and a more hawkish tone could offer the currency some relief. Tech and chip-related names remain the most sensitive part of the market to risk-off swings driven by Middle East headlines. --- Tokyo stocks are trading at the mercy of Middle East headlines and oil, while the BOJ is expected to sit tight this week and save its next moves for the new year.

title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6691 – Reuters estimate
body: The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point.
